text:
1.  A di-substituted benzene ring (C6H4) contributes 6 C, 4 H and 4 double-bond equivalents (DBE).

2.  The IR shows an ester, so “–CO₂–” must be present.  
    • carbonyl C = 1 C, 1 DBE  
    • –O–R alkoxy C (usually a –CH₃) = 1 C, 3 H

3.  The ¹H NMR gives six different kinds of protons:  
   • 2 aromatic signals ⇒ 4 aromatic H in two equivalent pairs (para-disubstituted ring).  
   • 2 vinyl-H signals (one d, one dq) ⇒ an –CH=CH– fragment in which one of the vinylic H’s (d) couples only to the other vinylic H, while the second vinylic H (dq) also couples to a neighbouring –CH₃ group.  
   • 2 CH₃ signals (one coupled to the vinylic H, one independent, e.g. a methoxy).

   Therefore the substituents can be:  
   a) –CO₂CH₃ (ester group)  
   b) –CH=CH–CH₃ (propenyl group)

4.  Counting atoms for p-(1-propenyl) methyl benzoate:

   Benzene ring ………………… 6 C, 4 H  
   Carbonyl carbon …………….. 1 C, 0 H  
   Methoxy carbon ……………… 1 C, 3 H  
   Propenyl group CH₃–CH=CH– … 3 C, 5 H  
   ---------------------------------------------  
   Total ………………………… 11 C, 12 H, O₂  

5.  Degree of unsaturation (DBE) for C₁₁H₁₂O₂:  
   DBE = C – H/2 + 1 = 11 – 12/2 + 1 = 6  
   (matches 4 from benzene + 1 carbonyl + 1 alkene).

6.  Among the options, C₁₁H₁₂O₂ (choice C) is the only formula with 11 carbons, 12 hydrogens, two oxygens and 6 DBE, and it is fully consistent with the NMR integrations (12 total H), the absence of CH₂ signals, and the presence of exactly two CH₃ groups.

Answer: C
